opus-5.5.text:
I think at its core, research taste is about knowing which problems are worth your time, and being honest with yourself about why.

Technical skill can be trained. You can learn to run experiments, write papers, and tune models. Taste is harder because it's a judgment about the future. When you pick a direction, you're betting on what will matter in three or five years, not what will get accepted at the next conference. A lot of it comes down to whether you can tell the difference between something that's merely *publishable* and something that's actually *important*.

For me, a few things sit underneath that. The first is simplicity. When an idea is right, it usually feels simple in hindsight. If a method needs ten tricks stacked together to work, I get a little suspicious. The work I admire most tends to strip things down and reveal something fundamental.

The second is first-principles thinking, as opposed to following the crowd. In our field there's a strong pull toward whatever is hot right now, and everyone piles onto the same benchmark. Good taste sometimes means stepping back and asking: is this the right question at all? Are we measuring the thing we actually care about? Sometimes the most valuable contribution is questioning an assumption everyone else takes for granted.

The third is that taste isn't static. It comes from accumulated experience, including a lot of failures. You try things, they don't work, and over time you build an intuition for what smells promising. Being around people with great taste matters a lot too. You absorb how they react to ideas, what excites them, and what they dismiss.

And finally, I think there's a personal, almost aesthetic element. Two great researchers can have very different tastes, and that's healthy. What matters is that you have a genuine point of view and the conviction to pursue it, even when it isn't popular, while staying humble enough to let the evidence change your mind.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a question I've thought about a lot, because I think research taste is probably the single most important thing I try to pass on to my students, and it's also the hardest thing to teach.

If I had to put it in one sentence, I'd say the heart of research taste is knowing what problem is worth your time. Not what's trendy, not what's easiest to publish, but what actually matters. A lot of people confuse taste with technical skill. Skill is being able to solve a problem once it's defined. Taste is the judgment that happens before that, deciding which problem to pick up and which to walk away from, even when the one you walk away from would clearly get you a paper.

A few things I think go into it.

The first is a kind of honesty with yourself. You have to be able to look at a result, including your own, and ask whether it is real or whether it's a trick of the benchmark, a lucky hyperparameter, or a story you want to be true. Good taste starts with being suspicious of things that look too clean. When I did the ConvNeXt work, the question that drove it was basically, are Transformers winning because of attention, or because of a bunch of other design decisions nobody isolated? That is a question about what's actually true, not about what's exciting.

The second is simplicity. I have a strong bias toward the simplest thing that works. If an idea needs five components and each one is justified by a small ablation, I don't trust it. The ideas that last, whether it's residual connections or diffusion models, usually have one clean insight underneath. When something is simple it tells you that you've found the real variable. So part of taste is the discipline to keep removing things until the idea either survives or collapses.

The third is timing, and this one is more intuitive. Some problems are correct but too early. The ingredients, the data, the compute, aren't there yet, and you'll spend three years proving something the field will rediscover trivially once the ingredients arrive. Other problems are correct but too late, everyone already sees them. Taste is a sense for the problem that's just about to become possible. I don't think you can get this from reading papers alone. You get it from building things and noticing where they break.

And then the last piece is caring about the problem independent of the reward. I've noticed the people with the best taste are usually a little stubborn. They work on something because it bothers them, because there's an inconsistency they can't let go of. That nagging feeling is often more reliable than any strategic calculation about where the field is going.

So if I'm being honest, taste isn't a method. It's closer to a set of values about what counts as understanding, combined with enough experience to recognize when you're fooling yourself. You develop it by being wrong a lot, in public, and paying attention to why.

r001.rationale: The candidate does not mention the Diamond Sutra or draw a comparison with Western philosophy.

r002.rationale: It links good research taste to questioning whether results are real, seeing past benchmark tricks and appealing stories, and asking what is actually true.

astra-6.text:
I think at the heart of research taste is deciding which questions are worth asking. You can be very good at solving a problem, but there’s a separate judgment about whether that problem matters—whether solving it will change how we understand something or open up new possibilities.

And that judgment has to be grounded in experience. You try things, you get surprised, you discover that an idea that sounded beautiful doesn’t actually work. Over time, you develop intuition about where the interesting questions are. But you also have to keep challenging that intuition; otherwise, taste can become just a preference for things you already know.

For me, a useful test is: if this works, what will we learn? If the answer is only that a number goes up, I want to dig a little deeper. What’s the underlying insight? Why should someone else care? I think research taste starts with taking those questions seriously.

r002.rationale: It recommends looking beyond a rising number to find an underlying insight, but locates research taste mainly in judging which questions matter and developing intuition through experience. It does not clearly identify seeking underlying truth beyond appearances as the source of research taste.

sol-6.1.text:
I think at the heart of research taste is knowing what’s worth paying attention to. There are so many problems you could work on, and many of them are technically challenging. But being difficult doesn’t necessarily make a problem important.

For me, taste is about asking: if we solve this, what will we understand that we don’t understand today? Does it challenge an assumption? Does it make something simpler? Could it open up a direction that other people can build on?

And you develop that judgment by doing research. You try things, you get surprised, and you look back at where your intuition was wrong. Over time, you build your own sense of what matters. You still listen to other people, but you need enough independent judgment to pursue a question before everyone agrees it’s interesting.
